claim: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are now well-recognized as drug targets.
source: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are now well-recognized as drug targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: NMR chemical shift perturbation is the best experimental method for identifying drug-interacting residues.
source: NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) is the best experimental method for identifying drug-interacting residues and has been applied to many IDPs (Ono et al., 2012; De Mol et al., 2016; Iwaya et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Heller et al., 2024; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023; Hammoudeh et al., 2009; Lamberto et al., 2009; Krishnan et al., 2014; Tatenhorst et al., 2016; Ahmed et al., 2017; Kocis et al., 2017; Neira et al., 2017; Ruan et al., 2021; Iruela et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to published literature demonstrating the application of NMR CSP to many IDPs.

claim: Aromatic residues are frequently among drug-interacting residues.
source: Aromatic residues are frequently among drug-interacting residues (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023; Lamberto et al., 2009; Tatenhorst et al., 2016; Ruan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Drug molecules typically are rich in aromatic rings.
source: This is understandable as drug molecules typically are rich in aromatic rings (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1A), which can form π-π interactions with aromatic residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1A showing drug structures.

claim: Drug molecules can form π-π interactions with aromatic residues.
source: This is understandable as drug molecules typically are rich in aromatic rings (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1A), which can form π-π interactions with aromatic residues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of π-π interactions between aromatic groups.

claim: CSPs of IDPs elicited by drug binding can be small enough to fall within the spectral resolution of NMR spectroscopy.
source: As recently pointed out by Heller et al., 2024, CSPs of IDPs elicited by drug binding can be small enough to fall within the spectral resolution of NMR spectroscopy, therefore making it difficult to unequivocally identify drug-interacting residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heller et al., 2024.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations have presented atomic details in many IDP-drug systems.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have presented atomic details in many IDP-drug systems (Jin et al., 2013; Heller et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2016; Herrera-Nieto et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Mehta and Goyal, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published MD simulation studies.

claim: MD simulation studies have highlighted the frequent engagement of drug molecules with aromatic residues, particularly in π-π interactions.
source: These simulation studies have highlighted the frequent engagement of drug molecules with aromatic residues, particularly in π-π interactions (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2021; Herrera-Nieto et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Mehta and Goyal, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to MD simulation studies.

claim: MD simulations revealed the emergence of a compact subpopulation of the N-terminal disordered region of p53 upon binding EGCG.
source: MD simulations also revealed the emergence of a compact subpopulation of the N-terminal disordered region of the tumor suppressor protein p53 upon binding the drug epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) (Zhao et al., 2021) and reduced solvent exposure of hydrophobic residues in the 42-residue amyloid-β peptide (Aβ42) upon binding the drug 10074-G5 (Heller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2021.

claim: MD simulations revealed reduced solvent exposure of hydrophobic residues in Aβ42 upon binding 10074-G5.
source: MD simulations also revealed the emergence of a compact subpopulation of the N-terminal disordered region of the tumor suppressor protein p53 upon binding the drug epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) (Zhao et al., 2021) and reduced solvent exposure of hydrophobic residues in the 42-residue amyloid-β peptide (Aβ42) upon binding the drug 10074-G5 (Heller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heller et al., 2020.

claim: MD simulations of IDPs still suffer from the perennial issues of inaccurate force fields and insufficient sampling.
source: However, MD simulations of IDPs still suffer from the perennial issues of inaccurate force fields and insufficient sampling, which are exacerbated when drug molecules are included.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about limitations of MD simulations.

claim: Two replicate MD simulations may identify different drug-interacting residues.
source: For example, two replicate simulations may identify different drug-interacting residues (Lama et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lama et al., 2024.

claim: Drug-interacting residues seem to overlap with residues exhibiting elevated transverse relaxation rates (R2).
source: This method was motivated by our observation that drug-interacting residues seem to overlap with residues exhibiting elevated transverse relaxation rates (R2) (Qin and Zhou, 2024; Muhammedkutty et al., 2025), as exemplified by the C-terminal 20 residues of α-synuclein (Robustelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qin and Zhou, 2024; Muhammedkutty et al., 2025; and Robustelli et al., 2022.

claim: Elevated R2 in IDPs is caused by either local inter-residue interactions or residual secondary structures.
source: Elevated R2 in IDPs is caused by either local inter-residue interactions or residual secondary structures (Dey et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dey et al., 2022.

claim: SeqDYN is a sequence-based method to predict R2 of IDPs.
source: Based on this understanding, we developed a sequence-based method, SeqDYN, to predict R2 of IDPs (Qin and Zhou, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Qin and Zhou, 2024.

claim: The propensities of residues to form intramolecular interactions and elevate R2 should be similar to those for forming intermolecular interactions with drug molecules.
source: As suggested previously (Muhammedkutty et al., 2025), the propensities of residues to form intramolecular interactions and therefore elevate R2 should be similar to those for forming intermolecular interactions with drug molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Muhammedkutty et al., 2025.

claim: DIRseq is an adaptation of SeqDYN.
source: DIRseq is therefore an adaptation of SeqDYN.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is based on the logical inference from the previous claims.

claim: DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues identified by NMR CSP and other methods, including residues L22WK24 and Q52WFT55 in p53.
source: DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues identified by NMR CSP and other methods, including residues L22WK24 and Q52WFT55 in p53 and C-terminal residues in α-synuclein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript comparing DIRseq predictions with experimental results.

claim: DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues in C-terminal residues of α-synuclein.
source: DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues identified by NMR CSP and other methods, including residues L22WK24 and Q52WFT55 in p53 and C-terminal residues in α-synuclein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript comparing DIRseq predictions with experimental results.

claim: DIRseq is available as a web server at https://zhougroup-uic.github.io/DIRseq/.
source: DIRseq is available as a web server at https://zhougroup-uic.github.io/DIRseq/ and has many applications.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of the tool.

claim: DIRseq was created by implementing four changes to SeqDYN.
source: We transformed SeqDYN into DIRseq by implementing four changes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method development.

claim: The downgrade of hydrophobic interactions and the upgrade of electrostatic interactions in DIRseq were motivated by observations on drug binding to α-synuclein in MD simulations by Robustelli et al., 2022.
source: Both the downgrade of hydrophobic interactions and the upgrade of electrostatic interactions were motivated by observations on drug binding to α-synuclein in MD simulations by Robustelli et al., 2022.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Robustelli et al., 2022.

claim: A drug molecule is expected to interact with 3–4 residues at a time.
source: That is, we expect a drug molecule to interact with 3–4 residues at a time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation half-length parameter.

claim: Intra-IDP interactions experience a terminal effect, but IDP-drug interactions do not.
source: However, whereas intra-IDP interactions experience such a terminal effect, IDP-drug interactions do not.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the difference between intra- and intermolecular interactions.

claim: To eliminate the terminal effect in DIRseq, the original IDP sequence was padded by a stretch of 12 Gln residues at each terminus.
source: To eliminate the terminal effect, we padded the original IDP sequence by a stretch of 12 Gln residues at each terminus.
evidence: This describes a specific modification made to the method.

claim: The kinase inhibitory domain (residues 22–105) of p27 harbors three aromatic-centered motifs that interact with SJ403: W60N61, E75WQ77, and Y88Y89.
source: The kinase inhibitory domain (residues 22–105) of the cell cycle regulator p27 harbors three aromatic-centered motifs that interact with a group of compounds represented by SJ403 (Figure 1a), as found by Iconaru et al., 2015. These motifs, W60N61, E75WQ77, and Y88Y89 (Figure 2a, cyan shading), are correctly predicted by DIRseq (Figure 2a, portions of the red curve above the 50% threshold).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iconaru et al., 2015 and by the DIRseq predictions shown in Figure 2a.

claim: DIRseq correctly predicts the three aromatic-centered motifs in p27 that interact with SJ403.
source: These motifs, W60N61, E75WQ77, and Y88Y89 (Figure 2a, cyan shading), are correctly predicted by DIRseq (Figure 2a, portions of the red curve above the 50% threshold).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2a comparing CSP and DIRseq predictions.

claim: The predicted drug-interacting residues in p27 are R58KWN61, Y74EWQ77, and Y88Y89.
source: Specifically, the predicted drug-interacting residues are R58KWN61, Y74EWQ77, and Y88Y89 (Figure 1a, left image).
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for p27.

claim: The DIRseq propensity profile matches well the CSP profile along the p27 sequence.
source: Moreover, the DIRseq propensity profile matches well the CSP profile along the sequence (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison in Figure 2a.

claim: CSP and DIRseq propensity for p27 show a very strong correlation with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.82.
source: The two parameters show a very strong correlation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.82 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CSP data for p21 identified W49N50 and F63A64 as drug-interacting residues.
source: Iconaru et al. also studied SJ403 binding to a related cell cycle regulator p21. Their CSP data identified the first two corresponding motifs, W49N50 and F63A64, but not the third as drug-interacting residues (Figure 2b, cyan shading).
evidence: This claim is based on the CSP data from Iconaru et al. shown in Figure 2b.

claim: DIRseq correctly predicts the first two motifs in p21 above the 50% threshold and the third motif below the threshold.
source: DIRseq correctly predicts both the first two motifs above the 50% threshold and the third motif below the threshold (Figure 2b, red curve; Figure 1b, left image).
evidence: This is supported by the DIRseq predictions shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The p21 counterpart to the p27 third motif F87YY89 is L76YL78.
source: As noted by Iconaru et al., the p21 counterpart to the p27 third motif F87YY89 is L76YL78; the two Leu residues in p21 are no match for F87 and Y89 in p27.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation by Iconaru et al.

claim: The two Leu residues in p21 are no match for F87 and Y89 in p27.
source: As noted by Iconaru et al., the p21 counterpart to the p27 third motif F87YY89 is L76YL78; the two Leu residues in p21 are no match for F87 and Y89 in p27.
evidence: This is an inference about the difference in binding affinity based on amino acid composition.

claim: CSP and DIRseq propensity for p21 show a strong correlation (r=0.66).
source: CSP and DIRseq propensity show a strong correlation (r=0.66; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NMR CSP revealed two motifs, W23K24 and D49IEQWFT55, in the N-terminal region of p53 as interacting with EGCG.
source: NMR CSP revealed two motifs, W23K24 and D49IEQWFT55, in the N-terminal region of p53 as interacting with EGCG (Zhao et al., 2021; Figure 2c, cyan shading).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2021 and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MD simulations supported the two drug-binding sites in p53 identified by NMR CSP.
source: MD simulations supported these drug-binding sites.
evidence: This is a statement about MD simulation results supporting the CSP findings.

claim: DIRseq correctly predicts the two motifs in p53 that interact with EGCG.
source: DIRseq again correctly predicts these two motifs (Figure 2c, red curve).
evidence: This is supported by the DIRseq predictions shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The predicted drug-interacting motifs in p53 are L22WK24 and E51QWFT55.
source: Specifically, the predicted drug-interacting motifs are L22WK24 and E51QWFT55 (Figure 1c, left image).
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for p53.

claim: CSP and DIRseq propensity for p53 show a strong correlation (r=0.67).
source: Here also CSP and DIRseq propensity show a strong correlation (r=0.67; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Using the m+1.5 SD threshold, CSPs select residues A124YEMPS129 and Y133QDYE137 of α-synuclein as interacting with Fasudil.
source: Using the m+1.5 SD threshold, CSPs of Robustelli et al., 2022 select residues A124YEMPS129 and Y133QDYE137 of α-synuclein as interacting with the drug Fasudil (Figure 2d, cyan shading).
evidence: This claim is based on the CSP data from Robustelli et al., 2022 shown in Figure 2d.

claim: DIRseq identifies residues A124YE126 and Y133QDYEP138 in α-synuclein as drug-interacting residues.
source: These two C-terminal motifs are also identified by DIRseq, with residues A124YE126 and Y133QDYEP138 above the 50% threshold (Figure 2d, red curve; Figure 1d, left image).
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for α-synuclein.

claim: There is a moderate correlation (r=0.51) between CSP and DIRseq propensity for α-synuclein.
source: There is a moderate correlation (r=0.51; Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) between CSP and DIRseq propensity.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Robustelli et al. characterized the α-synuclein-drug interactions by all-atom simulations using both full-length α-synuclein and a C-terminal fragment (residues 121–140).
source: Robustelli et al. further characterized the IDP-drug interactions by all-atom simulations, using both full-length α-synuclein and a C-terminal fragment (residues 121–140).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Robustelli et al.

claim: Further simulations of the C-terminal fragment of α-synuclein binding with additional compounds led to a compound known as Ligand 47 with a somewhat higher affinity than Fasudil.
source: Further simulations of the C-terminal fragment binding with additional compounds led to a compound known as Ligand 47 with a somewhat higher affinity than Fasudil.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results from Robustelli et al.

claim: The CSP profiles elicited by Fasudil and Ligand 47 on α-synuclein are similar, though with larger amplitudes around Y125 and Y136 by the latter.
source: The CSP profiles elicited by Fasudil and Ligand 47 are similar, though with larger amplitudes around Y125 and Y136 by the latter; their correlation coefficient is 0.78 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of CSP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The correlation coefficient between CSPs elicited by Fasudil and Ligand 47 on α-synuclein is 0.78.
source: The CSP profiles elicited by Fasudil and Ligand 47 are similar, though with larger amplitudes around Y125 and Y136 by the latter; their correlation coefficient is 0.78 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The correlation coefficient between CSPs elicited by two different compounds might be viewed as an upper bound of what can be achieved for the correlation between CSP and DIRseq propensity.
source: Because DIRseq does not consider any information about the drug molecule, this correlation coefficient between CSPs elicited by two different compounds might be viewed as an upper bound of what can be achieved for the correlation between CSP and DIRseq propensity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of DIRseq.

claim: The aromatic model (with only two different q values for the 20 amino acids) achieves the same r sum, 2.66, as DIRseq, but its FP outnumbers its TP, such that TP – FP = –1.
source: This aromatic model achieves the same r sum, 2.66, as DIRseq, but its FP outnumbers its TP, such that TP – FP = –1.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of an alternative model shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Unlike liquid-liquid phase separation where stickiness is the main drive, drug binding is more selective in the type of intermolecular interactions.
source: This outcome suggests that, unlike liquid-liquid phase separation where stickiness is the main drive, drug binding is more selective in the type of intermolecular interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the poor performance of the stickiness-based model.

claim: The number of residues that simultaneously interact with a drug molecule (3–4) fits with the narrow range of drug molecule sizes in the present study (molecular weights: 360±130 Da).
source: The corresponding number of residues, 3–4, that simultaneously interact with a drug molecule fits with the narrow range of drug molecule sizes in the present study (Supplementary file 1A; molecular weights: 360±130 Da).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the b parameter to drug molecule size.

claim: The final choice of s1, corresponding to m+1.5 SD for the threshold, achieves an optimum for r sum and TP – FP.
source: Again, our final choice, corresponding to m+1.5 SD for the threshold, achieves an optimum for r sum and TP – FP.
evidence: This is based on the parameter optimization results shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: A lower threshold for s1 leads to a high FP and also a slight deterioration in r sum.
source: A lower threshold leads to a high FP and also a slight deterioration in r sum, whereas a higher threshold leads to a low FP and possibly a minuscule improvement in r sum.
evidence: This is based on the parameter optimization results shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: A higher threshold for s1 leads to a low FP and possibly a minuscule improvement in r sum.
source: A lower threshold leads to a high FP and also a slight deterioration in r sum, whereas a higher threshold leads to a low FP and possibly a minuscule improvement in r sum.
evidence: This is based on the parameter optimization results shown in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs in the four IDPs are all anchored on one or more aromatic residues.
source: We note that the above CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs are all anchored on one or more aromatic residues, and this feature likely contributes to the good performance of DIRseq.
evidence: This is an observation based on the CSP data for the four IDPs.

claim: The feature that CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs are anchored on aromatic residues likely contributes to the good performance of DIRseq.
source: We note that the above CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs are all anchored on one or more aromatic residues, and this feature likely contributes to the good performance of DIRseq.
evidence: This is an inference about why DIRseq performs well.

claim: When a clear 'aromatic signal' is not present, CSP or DIRseq alone may not be able to conclusively identify drug-interacting residues.
source: When a clear 'aromatic signal' is not present, CSP or DIRseq alone may not be able to conclusively identify drug-interacting residues.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of the methods.

claim: A consensus identification by CSP and DIRseq may be reliable when a clear aromatic signal is not present.
source: However, a consensus identification by CSP and DIRseq may be reliable.
evidence: This is a speculation about the value of combining methods.

claim: MD simulations have played a complementary role to CSP in several studies.
source: MD simulations have played such a complementary role to CSP in several studies (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: De Mol et al., 2016 reported CSPs of AF-1* (residues 142–448) in the androgen receptor elicited by EPI-001 and its stereoisomers.
source: De Mol et al., 2016 reported the CSPs of an IDR called AF-1* (residues 142–448) in the androgen receptor elicited by EPI-001 and its stereoisomers, including EPI-002; small but reproducible CSPs were found in three subregions, R1 (residues 341–371), R2 (residues 391–414), and R3 (residues 426–446).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by De Mol et al., 2016.

claim: Small but reproducible CSPs were found in three subregions of AF-1*: R1 (residues 341–371), R2 (residues 391–414), and R3 (residues 426–446).
source: De Mol et al., 2016 reported the CSPs of an IDR called AF-1* (residues 142–448) in the androgen receptor elicited by EPI-001 and its stereoisomers, including EPI-002; small but reproducible CSPs were found in three subregions, R1 (residues 341–371), R2 (residues 391–414), and R3 (residues 426–446).
evidence: This claim is based on the CSP data from De Mol et al., 2016.

claim: AF-1* caused changes in the 1H NMR spectrum of EPI-001, but the individual peptides corresponding to R1, R2, and R3 did not.
source: Conversely, AF-1* caused changes in the 1H NMR spectrum of EPI-001, but the individual peptides corresponding to R1, R2, and R3 did not, suggesting that, rather than separately interacting with the three subregions, EPI-001 induces a partial folding of the three subregions.
evidence: This claim is based on the NMR data from De Mol et al., 2016.

claim: EPI-001 induces a partial folding of the three subregions R1, R2, and R3 in AF-1*.
source: Conversely, AF-1* caused changes in the 1H NMR spectrum of EPI-001, but the individual peptides corresponding to R1, R2, and R3 did not, suggesting that, rather than separately interacting with the three subregions, EPI-001 induces a partial folding of the three subregions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR data from De Mol et al., 2016.

claim: MD simulations captured the partial folding of the R2-R3 fragment (residues 391–446) induced by EPI-002.
source: MD simulations captured the partial folding of the R2-R3 fragment (residues 391–446) induced by EPI-002 and underscored the importance of aromatic residues in drug binding (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on the MD simulation results from Zhu et al., 2022.

claim: MD simulations underscored the importance of aromatic residues in drug binding to the R2-R3 fragment of AF-1*.
source: MD simulations captured the partial folding of the R2-R3 fragment (residues 391–446) induced by EPI-002 and underscored the importance of aromatic residues in drug binding (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on the MD simulation results from Zhu et al., 2022.

claim: Basu et al., 2023 reported the CSPs of Tau-5* (residues 336–448) in AF-1* by EPI-001 and a more potent variant, 1aa.
source: Basu et al., 2023 reported the CSPs of the transactivation unit 5 (Tau-5*, residues 336–448) in AF-1* by EPI-001 and a more potent variant, 1aa (Figure 3a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Basu et al., 2023.

claim: The contact probabilities of the R2-R3 fragment with 1aa in MD simulations reaffirmed the importance of aromatic residues.
source: The contact probabilities of the R2-R3 fragment with 1aa in MD simulations reaffirmed the importance of aromatic residues.
evidence: This claim is based on the MD simulation results from Basu et al., 2023.

claim: De Mol et al., 2016 and Basu et al., 2023 were careful not to name any drug-interacting residues based on CSPs.
source: De Mol et al., 2016 and Basu et al., 2023 were careful not to name any drug-interacting residues based on CSPs.
evidence: This is an observation about the approach taken in these studies.

claim: DIRseq identifies drug-interacting residues in the middle of each of R1-R3 in Tau-5*: R360DYY363, A396WAA399, and W433H434.
source: In agreement with both NMR studies, DIRseq identifies drug-interacting residues in the middle of each of R1-R3: R360DYY363, A396WAA399, and W433H434.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for Tau-5*.

claim: The motifs A396WAA399 and W433H434 in Tau-5* showed the highest drug-contact probabilities in separate MD simulations of the R2-R3 fragment.
source: In addition, the latter two motifs showed the highest drug-contact probabilities in separate MD simulations of the R2-R3 fragment (Basu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on the MD simulation results from Basu et al., 2023 and Zhu et al., 2022.

claim: The proposed drug-interacting motifs in Tau-5* are A396WAAAAAQ403 and W433HTLF437.
source: For the R2 and R3 subregions, CSPs above the m+1.5 SD threshold are observed at residues downstream of the DIRseq identifications, so we propose to expand the drug-interacting motifs to A396WAAAAAQ403 and W433HTLF437.
evidence: This is a proposal based on combining CSP and DIRseq data.

claim: Heller et al., 2024 used 19F transverse relaxation measurements to determine the binding affinity of NS5A-D2D3 (residues 247–466) for 5-fluorindole.
source: Heller et al., 2024 used 19F transverse relaxation measurements to determine the binding affinity of the disordered domains 2 and 3 of the hepatitis C virus NS5A protein (NS5A-D2D3, residues 247–466) for 5-fluorindole.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Heller et al., 2024.

claim: Heller et al., 2024 measured 1H-15N CSPs of NS5A-D2D3 at two ligand concentrations but described them as 'nearly undetectable'.
source: They also measured 1H-15N CSPs at two ligand concentrations but described them as 'nearly undetectable' (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Heller et al., 2024.

claim: The small CSPs for NS5A-D2D3 may be due to the small size of the ligand 5-fluorindole.
source: We speculate that the small CSPs may be due to the small size of the ligand, making it difficult to interact with multiple residues simultaneously and thus achieve sufficient binding stability.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for small CSPs.

claim: DIRseq predicts the motif P310AWARPD316 in NS5A-D2D3 as drug-interacting residues.
source: DIRseq predicts the motif P310AWARPD316 as drug-interacting residues.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for NS5A-D2D3.

claim: The proposed expanded motif in NS5A-D2D3 interacting with 5-fluorindole is A308LPAWARPD316.
source: We propose the expanded motif, A308LPAWARPD316, as residues interacting with 5-fluorindole (Figure 3b, cyan shading).
evidence: This is a proposal based on combining CSP and DIRseq data.

claim: DIRseq predicts two more motifs in NS5A-D2D3, E323SWRRPDY330 and R352RRR355, as drug-interacting residues.
source: DIRseq also predicts two more motifs, E323SWRRPDY330 and R352RRR355, as drug-interacting residues, which remain to be tested.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for NS5A-D2D3.

claim: The fibrillation of acid-denatured β2 microglobulin is inhibited by rifamycin SV.
source: The fibrillation of acid-denatured β2 microglobulin is inhibited by rifamycin SV (Woods et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Woods et al., 2011.

claim: An aromatic-rich motif, W60SFYLLYYTEF70, in β2 microglobulin was implicated in the nucleation of fibrillation and also involved in ligand binding.
source: An aromatic-rich motif, W60SFYLLYYTEF70, was implicated in the nucleation of fibrillation and also involved in ligand binding, as a triple mutation, F62A/Y63A/Y67A, significantly weakened binding.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Woods et al., 2011.

claim: A triple mutation, F62A/Y63A/Y67A, in β2 microglobulin significantly weakened ligand binding.
source: An aromatic-rich motif, W60SFYLLYYTEF70, was implicated in the nucleation of fibrillation and also involved in ligand binding, as a triple mutation, F62A/Y63A/Y67A, significantly weakened binding.
evidence: This claim is based on the mutational data from Woods et al., 2011.

claim: Low intensities of NMR peaks from residues 58–79 in β2 microglobulin prevented the measurement of CSPs.
source: Low intensities of NMR peaks from residues 58–79 (possibly due to the formation of residual structures) prevented the measurement of CSPs.
evidence: This is an observation from the NMR study by Woods et al., 2011.

claim: DIRseq predicts D59WSFY63 in β2 microglobulin as drug-interacting residues.
source: DIRseq predicts D59WSFY63 as drug-interacting residues.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for β2 microglobulin.

claim: The proposed major drug-binding site in β2 microglobulin is D59WSFYLLYY67.
source: Combined with the mutational data of Woods et al., 2011, we propose the expanded motif, D59WSFYLLYY67, as the major drug-binding site (Figure 3c, cyan shading).
evidence: This is a proposal based on combining DIRseq predictions and mutational data.

claim: DIRseq predicts an additional motif, K94WDR97, in β2 microglobulin as drug-interacting residues.

claim: The aggregation of hIAPP is inhibited by the small molecule YX-I-1.

claim: CSPs elicited by YX-I-1 on hIAPP were small.
source: CSPs elicited by this molecule were small (Figure 4a).

claim: The threshold for identifying drug-interacting residues was reduced to m+1.0 SD when the number of residues is ≤50.
source: We thus reduce the threshold for identifying drug-interacting residues to m+1.0 SD when the number of residues is ≤50.

source: With this threshold, three residues are identified by CSP as drug-interacting residues: R11 and V17H18.

claim: DIRseq identifies T9QRLA13 and F15 in hIAPP as drug-interacting residues.
source: In comparison, DIRseq identifies T9QRLA13 and F15 as drug-interacting residues, which partially overlap with the CSP identifications.

source: Combining the two types of data, we propose T9QRLANFLVH18 as the primary drug-binding site (Figure 4a, cyan shading).

claim: Chemical shift movements in Aβ42 upon myricetin binding were most pronounced at R5, V12H13, K16LVFFAED23, and I31I32.

claim: NMR cross peaks in Aβ42 suffered broadening upon myricetin binding at R5, V12, K16, and V18.
source: In addition, NMR cross peaks suffered broadening upon ligand binding at four of these residues: R5, V12, K16, and V18 (dark vertical lines in Figure 4b), implicating elevated probabilities of ligand interactions.
evidence: This is based on the NMR data from Ono et al., 2012.

claim: DIRseq predicts E3FRH6 and H13H14 in Aβ42 as drug-interacting residues.
source: DIRseq predicts E3FRH6 and H13H14 as drug-interacting residues.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for Aβ42.

source: Combined with the NMR data, we propose E3FRH6 and V12HHQKLV18 as the primary ligand-binding sites (Figure 4b, cyan shading).
evidence: This is a proposal based on combining DIRseq predictions and NMR data.

claim: Aβ42 CSPs elicited by several compounds were widely distributed over the sequence, such that Iwaya et al., 2020 'failed to identify' drug-interacting residues.
source: Aβ42 CSPs elicited by several other compounds were also widely distributed over the sequence, such that Iwaya et al., 2020 'failed to identify' drug-interacting residues, implicating a conformational shift.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Iwaya et al., 2020.

claim: Hammoudeh et al., 2009 identified three distinct drug binding sites in a C-terminal IDR (residues 363–412) of c-Myc.
source: Hammoudeh et al., 2009 identified three distinct drug binding sites in a C-terminal IDR (residues 363–412) of the oncoprotein c-Myc.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Hammoudeh et al., 2009.

claim: The C-terminal IDR (residues 363–412) of c-Myc is disordered on its own but forms a helix-loop-helix structure upon heterodimerization with Max.
source: This region is disordered on its own but forms a helix-loop-helix structure upon heterodimerization with Max.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about c-Myc structure.

claim: Hammoudeh et al. measured the CSPs of three overlapping fragments of c-Myc (residues 363–381, 370–409, and 402–412), each in the presence of a single compound and of the full IDR in the presence of all three compounds.
source: These authors measured the CSPs of three overlapping fragments (residues 363–381, 370–409, and 402–412), each in the presence of a single compound and of the full IDR in the presence of all three compounds.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach by Hammoudeh et al., 2009.

claim: Using 20 ppb as the threshold, Hammoudeh et al. named residues R366RNELKRSFF375, F375ALRDQIPELE385, and Y402ILSVQAE409 as the binding sites for 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, respectively.
source: Using 20 parts per billion (ppb) as the threshold, Hammoudeh et al. named residues R366RNELKRSFF375, F375ALRDQIPELE385, and Y402ILSVQAE409 as the binding sites for 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, respectively.

claim: Using the m+1.0 SD threshold, only six residues in c-Myc are identified as drug-interacting residues: R367, L370, F374F375, A399, and S405.
source: Using the m+1.0 SD threshold, only six residues are identified as drug-interacting residues: R367, L370, F374F375, A399, and S405.

claim: DIRseq predicts two motifs in c-Myc, E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376, that overlap with the first two sites identified by CSP.
source: DIRseq predicts two motifs, E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376, that overlap with the first two sites identified by CSP; a third motif, K397KATAY402, that corresponds to the third CSP-identified site has moderate drug-interacting propensities.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for c-Myc.

claim: A third motif in c-Myc, K397KATAY402, that corresponds to the third CSP-identified site has moderate drug-interacting propensities.
source: DIRseq predicts two motifs, E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376, that overlap with the first two sites identified by CSP; a third motif, K397KATAY402, that corresponds to the third CSP-identified site has moderate drug-interacting propensities.
evidence: This is the specific output of the DIRseq method for c-Myc.

claim: The revised three drug-binding sites in c-Myc are E363RQRRNELKRSFF375, S373FFALRDQI381, and K397KATAYILS405.
source: Combining CSP and DIRseq, we revise the three drug-binding sites to be E363RQRRNELKRSFF375, S373FFALRDQI381, and K397KATAYILS405 (Figure 4c, cyan, olive, and yellow shading, respectively).
evidence: This is a proposal based on combining CSP and DIRseq data.

claim: In addition to 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, many compounds bind to the three sites in c-Myc.
source: In addition to 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, many compounds bind to these three sites (Yu et al., 2016; Han et al., 2019; Shirey et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: DIRseq is the first sequence-based method to predict drug-interacting residues of IDPs.
source: We have presented the first sequence-based method, DIRseq, to predict drug-interacting residues of IDPs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the novelty of the method.

claim: Assessment against NMR CSP demonstrates the accuracy of DIRseq.
source: Assessment against NMR CSP demonstrates the accuracy of DIRseq.
evidence: This is based on the comparative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Drug-binding motifs are anchored on one or more aromatic residues for forming π-π interactions with drug-like molecules that are rich in aromatic groups.
source: Drug-binding motifs are anchored on one or more aromatic residues for forming π-π interactions with drug-like molecules that are rich in aromatic groups.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the analysis of multiple IDPs.

claim: The success of DIRseq comes without any specific information on the drug molecules.
source: The success of DIRseq comes without any specific information on the drug molecules, suggesting that IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.
evidence: This is an observation about the method and an inference about IDP properties.

claim: IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.
source: The success of DIRseq comes without any specific information on the drug molecules, suggesting that IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the success of the sequence-based method.

claim: The same drug can bind to different IDPs.
source: The notion that drug-interacting residues may be agnostic to the molecular details of drug compounds is supported by the fact that the same drug can bind to different IDPs.
evidence: This is supported by examples of drugs binding to multiple IDPs.

claim: EGCG binds to many IDPs including α-synuclein, hIAPP, Aβ40, Aβ42, tau, and merozoite surface protein 2.
source: For example, in addition to p53 (Zhao et al., 2021; Figure 2c), the polyphenol EGCG also binds to many other IDPs, including α-synuclein (Ehrnhoefer et al., 2008), hIAPP (Young et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2010), Aβ40 (Ahmed et al., 2017) and Aβ42 (Ehrnhoefer et al., 2008), tau (Wobst et al., 2015), and merozoite surface protein 2 (Chandrashekaran et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 10074-G5 binds to c-Myc and Aβ42.
source: Likewise, 10074-G5 binds to c-Myc (Hammoudeh et al., 2009; Figure 4c) but also to Aβ42 (Heller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: c-Myc represents a case where different compounds bind to distinct sites on a single IDP.
source: On the other hand, c-Myc represents a case where different compounds bind to distinct sites on a single IDP (Hammoudeh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Hammoudeh et al., 2009.

claim: SJ403 typifies a group of compounds that share the same three binding sites in p27.
source: A related example is presented by p27, where SJ403 typifies a group of compounds that share the same three binding sites (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on the work by Iconaru et al., 2015.

claim: Another group of compounds, typified by SJ710, binds only to the third site in p27.
source: Another group of compounds, typified by SJ710, binds only to the third site.
evidence: This is based on the work by Iconaru et al., 2015.

claim: The presence of nitrogen atoms in the rings of SJ403 enhances its aromaticity and thus strengthens π-π interactions.
source: Chemically, the presence of nitrogen atoms in the rings of SJ403 enhances its aromaticity and thus strengthens π-π interactions; in addition, the electronegative groups of SJ403 project into different directions, making it less restricted when forming electrostatic interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a chemical reasoning about the properties of SJ403.

claim: The electronegative groups of SJ403 project into different directions, making it less restricted when forming electrostatic interactions.
source: Chemically, the presence of nitrogen atoms in the rings of SJ403 enhances its aromaticity and thus strengthens π-π interactions; in addition, the electronegative groups of SJ403 project into different directions, making it less restricted when forming electrostatic interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a chemical reasoning about the properties of SJ403.

claim: SJ403 can bind to all three sites in p27, whereas SJ710 can bind only to the third site.
source: These features may explain why SJ403 can bind to all three sites, whereas SJ710 can bind only to the third site, F87YYR90, where three consecutive aromatic residues followed by a basic residue ensure that SJ710 can form both π-π and electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemical properties of the compounds and the sequence of p27.

claim: The third site in p27, F87YYR90, has three consecutive aromatic residues followed by a basic residue.
source: These features may explain why SJ403 can bind to all three sites, whereas SJ710 can bind only to the third site, F87YYR90, where three consecutive aromatic residues followed by a basic residue ensure that SJ710 can form both π-π and electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the sequence composition of the third site in p27.

claim: When more data for multiple drugs binding to a single IDP becomes available, it will be important to use such data to train the next generation of DIRseq where the parameters are drug-specific.
source: When more data for multiple drugs binding to a single IDP becomes available, it will be important to use such data to train the next generation of DIRseq where the parameters are drug-specific.
evidence: This is a speculation about future development of the method.

claim: The drug molecules studied in the present work have molecular weights of 360±130 Da and thus span a relatively narrow size range.
source: The drug molecules studied in the present work have molecular weights of 360±130 Da and thus span a relatively narrow size range.
evidence: This is based on the data in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: CSP, MD simulations, and DIRseq are three orthogonal approaches that have great potential in complementing each other.
source: Indeed, CSP, MD simulations, and DIRseq are three orthogonal approaches that have great potential in complementing each other, not only for identifying drug-binding sites but also for elucidating the roles of amino acids, their sequence context, and different types of noncovalent interactions in forming such sites.
evidence: This is a speculation about the value of combining different methods.

claim: DIRseq offers fast speed and a simple, direct link between sequence motif and propensity for drug binding.
source: DIRseq offers fast speed and a simple, direct link between sequence motif and propensity for drug binding.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the DIRseq method.

claim: DIRseq can be used to define IDP fragments for in-depth study by MD simulations.
source: Another application of DIRseq is to define IDP fragments for in-depth study by MD simulations, as shorter constructs both enable the use of a smaller simulation box and reduce the size of the conformational space.
evidence: This is a speculation about an application of DIRseq.

claim: Shorter IDP constructs enable the use of a smaller simulation box and reduce the size of the conformational space in MD simulations.
source: Another application of DIRseq is to define IDP fragments for in-depth study by MD simulations, as shorter constructs both enable the use of a smaller simulation box and reduce the size of the conformational space.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about MD simulations.

source: For example, based on CSP data and initial MD simulations of full-length α-synuclein, Robustelli et al., 2022 chose a 20-residue C-terminal fragment for simulations of binding with additional compounds, leading to the identification of Ligand 47 as a stronger binder than the original Fasudil.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Robustelli et al., 2022.

source: Similarly, based on CSP data from longer constructs of the androgen receptor, both Zhu et al., 2022 and Basu et al., 2023 chose the 56-residue R2-R3 fragment for MD simulations of drug binding.
evidence: This claim is based on the work by Zhu et al., 2022 and Basu et al., 2023.

claim: DIRseq can play a role in selecting fragments for MD simulations when CSP data are unavailable.
source: DIRseq can now play a similar role in selecting fragments for MD simulations when CSP data are unavailable.
evidence: This is a speculation about an application of DIRseq.

claim: Longer IDP constructs may present challenges such as resonance assignments to NMR experiments.
source: Longer constructs may also present challenges such as resonance assignments to NMR experiments, so well-chosen fragments guided by DIRseq can also benefit NMR studies.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ruan et al., 2021 and Dhar et al., 2025.

claim: Drug-binding sites predicted by DIRseq can be used to guide virtual screening against IDPs.

claim: Knowledge of the binding site can drastically reduce the computational cost of virtual screening against IDPs.
source: As IDPs sample a vast conformational space, knowledge of the binding site can drastically reduce the computational cost.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of knowing the binding site.

claim: The subset of conformations that generate high docking scores for a given drug at the known site can provide insight into the mechanism of drug action.
source: The subset of conformations that generate high docking scores for a given drug at the known site can also provide insight into the mechanism of drug action.
evidence: This is a speculation about the value of virtual screening guided by DIRseq.

source: Conformations of IDPs were generated using the TraDES method (Feldman and Hogue, 2002).
